title: THEY WERE ORDINARY MEN—UNTIL THEIR ENEMIES REALIZED WHERE THEY HAD BEEN
paragraphs:
THEY WERE ORDINARY MEN—UNTIL THEIR ENEMIES REALIZED WHERE THEY HAD BEEN
Peter and John had no elite religious credentials, no prestigious position, and no human reason to intimidate Jerusalem’s most powerful religious court. But when they opened their mouths, the men judging them were astonished. Then came the realization they could not ignore: “They had been with Jesus.”
There is a terrifying question hidden inside Acts 4:13.
Not terrifying because it speaks of judgment.
Terrifying because it forces every person who calls himself a Christian to confront something far more personal:
If nobody knew you went to church... would anyone know you had been with Jesus?
Not because of the Bible verse in your biography.
Not because you occasionally post something Christian.
Not because you own a Bible, know worship songs, understand Christian vocabulary, or can tell people what denomination you belong to.
If all of that disappeared tonight...
Would there still be something about your life that made Jesus difficult to deny?
That question becomes even more piercing when you see the men standing at the center of Acts 4.
Ordinary men standing before extraordinary power.
Only hours earlier, something impossible had happened.
Acts 3 tells us about a man who had been unable to walk from birth. He was carried regularly to the temple gate called Beautiful, where he begged from those entering.
Other people walked past him on legs he had never been able to use.
And what Peter said has echoed through nearly two thousand years:
“Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee.”
Then Peter commanded him in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth to rise and walk.
Peter took him by the hand.
Then he entered the temple praising God.
The man who had spent years outside being carried was suddenly inside walking under his own strength.
This wasn't an anonymous stranger appearing with an unverifiable story. The people recognized the man who had been sitting at the gate begging.
He refused to steal the glory.
He essentially asked them: Why are you looking at us as though our own power or holiness made this man walk?
Peter immediately pointed them toward Jesus.
That detail destroys an enormous amount of counterfeit Christianity.
The evidence that someone has been with Jesus is not that people become impressed with that person.
The evidence is that through that person's life, people are confronted with Christ.
Peter did not build a platform around the miracle.
He preached the crucified and risen Jesus.
The priests, the captain of the temple, and the Sadducees confronted Peter and John. They were disturbed that the apostles were teaching the people and proclaiming resurrection in Jesus.
They had watched a disabled man walk.
They had watched a crowd gather.
Following Jesus had not made their lives safer.
It had made obedience more costly.
The next day, rulers, elders, scribes, and members of the high-priestly family assembled.
Peter and John were brought before them.
This was not a casual theological conversation.
Religious authority examining men who possessed neither their education nor their institutional standing.
By what power, or by what name, have you done this?
And then Scripture says something that changes everything.
Peter was filled with the Holy Spirit.
That cannot be removed from this story.
Peter's courage was not a motivational technique.
It was not self-confidence disguised as Christianity.
The same Peter who once collapsed under pressure was now standing under pressure proclaiming Jesus.
And that makes this scene almost unbearably beautiful.
Peter knew what it was to speak confidently and then crumble.
On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter had insisted that even if everyone else fell away, he would remain faithful.
And Peter remembered what Jesus had said.
Luke tells us Peter went out and wept bitterly.
The memory of his own voice saying he did not know Jesus.
The man who promised courage discovered how frightened he really was.
But Peter's story did not end beside that fire.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
Grace did not pretend Peter's failure never happened.
Jesus did not discard the disciple who denied Him.
He is standing before powerful men who have the ability to threaten him.
And he is speaking about Jesus.
There is salvation in no one else.
Grace does not merely forgive your past.
Grace can transform what your past convinced you that you would always be.
The denier can become a preacher.
The ashamed can become a witness.
The scandal does not have to become the final chapter.
And then we reach that breathtaking thirteenth verse.
Θεωροῦντες δὲ τὴν τοῦ Πέτρου παρρησίαν καὶ Ἰωάννου... ἐθαύμαζον, ἐπεγίνωσκόν τε αὐτοὺς ὅτι σὺν τῷ Ἰησοῦ ἦσαν.
At the heart of the sentence are several words worth slowing down for.
Boldness. Frankness. Freedom or confidence in speaking.
Then Luke describes Peter and John as:
These words have sometimes been made to sound as though the council thought Peter and John were stupid.
They were recognized as men without the formal scholarly training and status associated with the learned religious elite—ordinary, common men.
They were not members of Jerusalem's intellectual establishment.
They did not possess the credentials the council expected from men speaking with this kind of theological confidence.
Because these supposedly ordinary men were not behaving ordinarily.
The council could categorize their social position.
They could recognize their lack of elite scholarly credentials.
But they could not easily explain their courage.
ἐπεγίνωσκόν τε αὐτοὺς ὅτι σὺν τῷ Ἰησοῦ ἦσαν.
that they had been with Jesus.
Something had happened to these ordinary men because they had lived in proximity to an extraordinary Savior.
And now the fingerprints of that relationship were showing.
But there is something else in the room that day.
Something almost impossible to preach around.
Acts 4:14 says the healed man was standing there with Peter and John.
Sometimes the most devastating argument for the power of God is a transformed life standing in the room.
The council could debate Peter's theology.
Scripture says they had nothing to say in opposition.
There are moments when transformation speaks louder than argument.
And this is where Acts 4 stops being merely a story about two apostles and begins walking uncomfortably toward us.
Because many of us desperately want God to use us...
but secretly believe He cannot because we are too ordinary.
“Just somebody trying to survive another week.”
Acts 4 does not teach that learning is bad.
Scripture never gives us permission to glorify ignorance. Christians should love God with their minds, handle His Word faithfully, seek wisdom, and refuse careless interpretations.
But Acts 4 destroys the idea that God is restricted to people whom society considers impressive.
But God is not dependent upon any of them.
Peter and John's ultimate distinction was not that they lacked credentials.
It was that they had been with Jesus.
And maybe that is what your exhausted soul needed to hear.
You have spent years comparing yourself with people whose gifts seem larger than yours.
And somewhere along the way you quietly concluded:
“God could never use someone like me.”
The man who spoke too quickly.
The man who sank after stepping onto the water.
The man who rebuked Jesus and was himself sharply rebuked.
The man who promised loyalty and then denied knowing Christ.
And suddenly the question was no longer:
“What can Jesus do with a surrendered Peter?”
That question belongs to you too.
What could Jesus do with a surrendered you?
Not the imaginary version of you.
Not the version with more money.
The person reading these words while carrying things nobody else can see.
You with that prayer you almost stopped praying.
You with the sin you are ashamed to confess.
You with the wound you keep covering with “I'm fine.”
You with the fear that God must be disappointed every time He looks at you.
Jesus did not go to the cross for the imaginary, improved version of you.
The Gospel begins precisely where pretending ends.
And perhaps that is the deeper confrontation of Acts 4:13.
We can learn Christian language without living close to Christ.
We can attend church and remain spiritually distant.
We can post Scripture while secretly starving.
We can defend Christianity online while neglecting Christ in private.
We can know worship lyrics without worshiping.
We can become familiar with sermons without becoming familiar with surrender.
We can know things about Jesus without actually walking with Jesus.
“These men have obviously read many inspirational quotations.”
So ask yourself the question nobody else can answer for you.
Not merely when life fell apart.
When there is nothing to post?
Does your private life know the Jesus your public life talks about?
That question is not meant to drive you into despair.
Because the Jesus who restored Peter still receives repentant sinners.
If your prayer life has become almost nonexistent...
If sin has been slowly hardening your heart...
If you have spent months performing Christianity while privately drifting from Christ...
you do not need a better performance.
The Christian life was never supposed to be an attempt to look impressive enough for God.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive language.
“Jesus, I have been around Christian things, but I haven't been close to You.”
“Jesus, take what is left of me.”
And perhaps someday someone who knew the old you will notice something they cannot quite explain.
The anger does not own you anymore.
The addiction no longer has the final word.
You no longer need everybody's approval.
And eventually the explanation becomes impossible to separate from the name:
Not ordinary people pretending to be extraordinary.
Ordinary sinners being redeemed by an extraordinary Savior.
Peter and John were not the heroes of Acts 4.
The healed man pointed toward Jesus.
The apostles' courage pointed toward Jesus.
Their salvation message pointed toward Jesus.
So please don't finish this article thinking, “I need to become more impressive.”
Open His Word when nobody is watching.
Love people who cannot repay you.
And when you fail, do not make peace with sin—but do not run away from the Savior either.
Peter's story proves that failure surrendered to Jesus does not have to become your identity.
There was a courtyard in Peter's history.
But there was also an empty tomb.
And now I want to ask you for something deeper than a reaction button.
If this exposed something you have been hiding from God, don't manufacture a polished testimony.
You don't have to explain the details.
Sometimes three honest words are the beginning of coming out of isolation.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer desperately needs tonight.
The son who stopped believing he belongs.
The wife who feels spiritually alone.
The believer who failed and thinks Jesus no longer wants them.
The skeptic who believes Christianity is merely religion and rules.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered in obedience to Him.
And there is something even more important than merchandise.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen.
Because there may come a night when you feel ordinary again.
A night when failure starts speaking.
A night when your past starts reading its accusations aloud.
The ordinary man standing before extraordinary power because an extraordinary Savior had changed him.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not miss the Person at the center of it.
The Son of God who was crucified for sinners and raised from the dead.
and the Savior who restored Peter anyway.
Maybe you have spent too long trying to erase your scandal.
Because the world does not desperately need another Christian who knows how to look impressive.
It needs believers whose lives make people wonder where their courage came from...
how they survived what should have destroyed them...
how they still worship after everything they lost...
how they could possibly be forgiven after everything they did...
until finally there is only one explanation left:
And perhaps the greatest thing anyone could ever notice about your life is not that you became somebody...
but that somewhere along the way, it became impossible to look at you without seeing evidence that you had been with Someone.
Stay close enough to Jesus that even the scars of your scandal begin telling the story of His grace.
